landing.intro: Tinnitus attracts bold claims: miracle frequencies, 30-second fixes, “ear formulas”, new cures. Some contain a real kernel. This section takes the claims people actually meet, traces them to the original research, and gives each an evidence verdict. It is education, not medical advice, and verdicts describe the evidence rather than the people making the claims.

entry.title: Tinnitus claims: fact vs. evidence
entry.text: Frequencies, 30-second fixes, supplements, “cure discovered” headlines: each judged against the research, with an evidence verdict.

verdicts.name: Supported
verdicts.meaning: Good-quality evidence, ideally repeated by independent research groups, supports the claim as it is usually stated.
verdicts.notmean: It does not mean the approach works for everyone, is risk-free, or that the evidence cannot change.

verdicts.name: Partly Supported
verdicts.meaning: A real part of the claim holds up, but the claim as it is usually made goes further than the evidence does.
verdicts.notmean: It does not mean the claim is “half right” in a way that makes the rest acceptable. We say which part holds up and which does not.

verdicts.name: Misleading
verdicts.meaning: The claim contains a real kernel, but the usual way it is presented leads people to a wrong conclusion, for example by treating temporary relief as a cure, a result in mice as a human treatment, or a questionnaire improvement as a quieter sound.
verdicts.notmean: It does not mean the person making the claim intends to mislead. We judge the claim, not the speaker.

verdicts.name: Unsupported
verdicts.meaning: We found no good evidence for the claim. This covers two quite different situations: the claim was tested and did not show a benefit, or it has not been tested well enough to know. Each claim page says which applies.
verdicts.notmean: Unsupported does not necessarily mean disproven. It means the evidence needed to believe the claim is missing. A claim can be unsupported today and supported after better research.

verdicts.name: Insufficient Evidence
verdicts.meaning: There is too little, too small or too inconsistent evidence to say yes or no. Early or conflicting findings are in this group.
verdicts.notmean: It does not mean the approach fails, or that it works. It means we cannot tell yet, and more research could change the answer.

terms: How loud or intrusive the tinnitus sound itself is, usually rated by the person or matched to an external sound. A treatment that lowers loudness changes the sound.
How much tinnitus upsets, worries or frustrates a person. It is measured by questionnaires (for example the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory) and can improve while the sound stays the same.
How much tinnitus interferes with sleep, concentration, work, hearing in noise and relationships (for example the Tinnitus Functional Index).
Feeling better for a short time, such as while a masking sound plays or for hours afterwards. It is real, but it is not the same as lasting change.
Benefit that is still present weeks or months after a treatment, measured against a comparison group.
Tinnitus that is gone and stays gone because of the treatment, shown in controlled studies and repeated independently. No treatment has met this standard for tinnitus.
how: We judge each claim as it is commonly stated, not the topic in general. A topic can contain true statements and misleading ones, so each page also gives a verdict for each part of the claim.
We rely on primary sources: the trials and reviews themselves, guideline texts, regulator records and trial registries. Every page lists them, with links.
We keep loudness, distress, functional impact, temporary relief, sustained improvement and cure apart, because a claim often wins its credibility by blurring them.

We date every page. “Evidence through” is the date up to which we searched; “last reviewed” is when we last checked the page against its sources. A “first published” date appears only once a page is public. Verdicts can change when new evidence appears, and corrections are logged on our methodology page.

We name a product, company or person only when a regulator, a published study or a documented fact-check supports the specific statement, and we do not accuse anyone of fraud. We distinguish “tested and shown not to help” from “never tested”.

claims.question: Can a Certain Sound Frequency or “Hz” Video Cure Tinnitus?
claims.claim: “A specific frequency, such as 432 Hz, 528 Hz or a binaural-beat track, can retrain your brain and cure your tinnitus, and a free video can do it.”
claims.verdictLine: Sound can give real, temporary relief. Nothing in the research shows that a particular frequency or a video permanently cures tinnitus.
claims.metaTitle: Can a Sound Frequency or Hz Video Cure Tinnitus? The Evidence | Tinnitus Evidence
claims.metaDesc: 432 Hz, 528 Hz, binaural beats and notched sound: what the research shows about tinnitus sound claims, temporary relief versus lasting change, and what to look for.
claims.answer:
Sound can change how tinnitus feels while you listen. That part is real, and it is why sound is used in tinnitus clinics. What is not supported is the idea that one “healing” frequency, or a video, removes tinnitus for good.

  • 432 Hz and 528 Hz: we found no published human tinnitus-treatment trials specifically evaluating these frequencies (PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches, 15 October 2026).
  • Binaural beats: two small studies found no clear advantage over the same sound without the beats.[1, 2]
  • Notched (“gap”) music: an early small study was positive, but larger controlled trials mostly did not find it better than ordinary music.[3, 4, 5, 6]
  • Masking and sound enrichment: regulators accept sound devices for temporary relief, and guidelines disagree about longer-term value.[7, 8, 9, 10, 11]

“Unsupported” here does not mean every sound has been shown not to work. For 432 Hz and 528 Hz, it means we found no published human trials of them for tinnitus, not that they have been shown not to work.
subverdicts: “A sound or video can cure tinnitus”
Unsupported
No sound-based approach has been shown to remove tinnitus permanently. Trials report group averages, not cures.
“432 Hz / 528 Hz ‘healing’ frequencies work”
Insufficient Evidence
We found no published human tinnitus-treatment trials specifically evaluating these frequencies. Not shown to work; not shown to fail.
“Binaural beats reduce tinnitus”
Insufficient Evidence
Two small studies; the beats did not do better than the same sound without them.
“Notched or custom music retrains the brain”
Insufficient Evidence
One small positive study; later, larger trials did not show an advantage over ordinary music.
“Sound can give temporary relief”
Partly Supported
Sound can cover or reduce tinnitus while it plays; regulators clear devices for “temporary relief”. Lasting benefit is not shown.

sections: What “Hz” claims are really claiming

Hertz (Hz) is the pitch of a tone. Tinnitus pitch differs from person to person, and we found no research linking a tone chosen for its supposed “healing” properties to a person’s tinnitus. The 432 Hz and 528 Hz claims we found in videos rest on assertion, not on tinnitus research: searches of PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov on 15 October 2026 for tinnitus with either number found no human tinnitus-treatment trial specifically evaluating either frequency (the few PubMed hits were unrelated papers).

Clinical sound research uses frequencies matched to a person’s own tinnitus or hearing loss, tested against a comparison sound. That is a different thing from a single “universal” frequency.
What sound can do: masking and temporary relief

A tinnitus masker is a regulated medical device. U.S. regulations describe it as a device “intended to generate noise of sufficient intensity and bandwidth to mask ringing in the ears”, in Class II.[7] Cleared sound devices are indicated for the temporary relief of tinnitus symptoms, for use as part of a management programme with a hearing professional.[8, 12]

Some people also get a short-lived drop in tinnitus loudness after certain sounds. In one laboratory study of 20 people with chronic tinnitus, at least one of 17 sounds reduced loudness in 90% of them, most often amplitude-modulated tones near the tinnitus pitch. The authors described this as temporary and said the long-term effects remained to be investigated.[13]
Does long-term listening help? Reviews and guidelines disagree

Cochrane reviewers looked for controlled trials of sound devices. In 2012 they found six trials (553 people) and no significant change in tinnitus loudness or overall severity compared with other approaches, adding that the absence of conclusive evidence “should not be interpreted as evidence of lack of effectiveness”.[14] A 2018 Cochrane review of hearing aids and sound generators found eight studies (590 people) and no data on the main comparisons against waiting list, placebo or information only.[15]

Guidelines read the same gap differently:

  • The 2026 U.S. guideline says clinicians may recommend sound enrichment (an option, not a firm recommendation).[9]
  • The 2019 European guideline says sound therapy “may be useful for acute relief purposes but is not considered an effective intervention with long-term results”.[16]
  • The German guideline says sound therapy “should not be practiced”, noting that comparison conditions are often missing and changes may reflect normal habituation.[10]
  • The UK’s NICE guideline made no recommendation on sound therapy and called for research.[11]

Taken together: sound is a reasonable comfort tool for many people, and we found no study showing that it is a cure.
Binaural beats

A binaural beat is an illusion: two slightly different tones, one in each ear, make you hear a pulsing third tone. Two small studies tested it. In 20 adults, an 8 Hz binaural beat added to ocean sound showed no significant group benefit beyond the ocean sound alone.[1] In a trial of 30 men, listening for 15 minutes twice a day for four weeks, both the music-only group and the music-plus-beats group improved on tinnitus questionnaires, and the groups did not differ on nearly every measure; the authors wrote that the study “failed to demonstrate the superiority” of adding beats.[2]

That both groups improved is the point: relaxing sound, time and expectation can all lower how much tinnitus bothers a person, which is why a comparison group is essential.
Notched music and “brain retraining” sounds

Notched music removes a band of frequencies around the tinnitus pitch, on the theory that the brain’s overactive area calms down. The first small controlled study (16 people, 12 months of listening) reported reduced loudness and reduced auditory-cortex activity.[3] Later trials were less encouraging. In a double-blind trial of 100 people, 3 months of listening did not change the main outcomes.[4] A trial of 104 people found no significant difference in handicap scores against ordinary music.[5] A 2024 meta-analysis of three studies (99 notched-music and 109 comparison participants) found no significant difference in distress against listening to music, with the authors calling for more research.[6] The German guideline recommends against it.[10]

Newer designs are still being tested. In a 2025 blinded online crossover trial, 53 people who completed it reported lower tinnitus loudness after a specially modulated sound but not after a near-identical sham sound, while distress fell in both periods; the authors list further optimisation as the next step.[17] That is an encouraging early result from one study, not an established treatment.
Why a video can feel like it works

Tinnitus naturally rises and falls. Many people also feel better simply from relaxing, from sleeping better, or from expecting relief. In the binaural-beat trial above and in the 2025 online trial, distress improved in the comparison condition too. A video that makes you feel calmer for an hour has done something real, but it has not shown that it changed the underlying tinnitus.
distinctions: Is the tinnitus sound itself quieter?
Brief reductions during or just after some sounds. Lower rated loudness in a few small trials, not consistently across controlled trials.
How much does it upset or worry me?
Often improves with sound, but comparison groups improve too, so it cannot be credited to a particular frequency.
Does it disrupt sleep, focus or daily life?
Sound can help some people sleep or concentrate. Studies of any single frequency are lacking.
Plausible and accepted by regulators for masking devices.
Still better weeks or months later
Not shown for any single frequency or video. Mixed results for notched music; early results for newer designs.
No published evidence for any sound.
claims.limits: Sound studies are mostly small and short, use different questionnaires and comparison sounds, and are hard to blind (you can tell what you are hearing). Several programmes were designed by the people who tested them or by companies that sell them, so funding and independence matter; each treatment page on this site rates them. Most “Hz” claims have no study behind them at all, so there is nothing to appraise. One 2025 trial received a different participant count in press coverage than in its published abstract; we use the abstract.

claims.practical:
• If tinnitus is new, in one ear, pulsing, or comes with hearing loss or dizziness, have it checked by a clinician first. A hearing test is the usual starting point.[9]
  • Low-level background sound at bedtime or in quiet rooms is a sensible, low-risk comfort measure for many people. Keep volume comfortable, never loud enough to risk hearing damage, and stop if it makes tinnitus worse.
  • If tinnitus bothers you, the best-supported approaches target distress: cognitive behavioural therapy (recommended in both the 2026 U.S. and 2019 European guidelines) and a hearing-aid evaluation for people with hearing difficulties (recommended in the 2026 U.S. guideline).[9, 16]
  • Be cautious of any recording promising a cure, a “universal” frequency, or results in minutes, and of anything that asks you to pay for it.

claims.question: Can a 30-Second Neck or Jaw Move Stop Tinnitus?
claims.claim: “One quick neck, jaw or pressure-point move can silence the ringing in about 30 seconds.”
claims.verdictLine: For some people tinnitus really does change with neck or jaw movement. A quick move that stops it has not been shown to work, and forceful neck manipulation carries its own risks.
claims.metaTitle: Can a 30-Second Neck or Jaw Move Stop Tinnitus? The Evidence | Tinnitus Evidence
claims.metaDesc: Somatic (somatosensory) tinnitus is real for some people, but quick neck or jaw moves are not proven to stop it. What physiotherapy trials show, and safety points.
claims.safety:
Safety first. Do not twist, crack, hold or force your neck to try to stop tinnitus. Forceful neck manipulation has been linked, rarely, to tears in the arteries of the neck (cervical artery dissection), a cause of stroke. An American Heart Association / American Stroke Association statement reports that most population studies find an association between manipulative neck therapy and vertebral-artery stroke in young patients, while stating that the evidence is insufficient to establish that manipulation causes the tears.[1]

Call emergency services right away (911 in the U.S.) for stroke signs: sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm or leg, sudden confusion or trouble speaking, sudden trouble seeing, sudden trouble walking, dizziness or loss of balance, or a sudden severe headache with no known cause.[2] The same AHA/ASA statement lists one-sided headache, neck pain and pulsatile (heartbeat-like) tinnitus among the ways an artery tear can show itself, so get urgent medical assessment if these appear, especially after a neck injury or neck manipulation.[1] The UK’s NICE guideline says tinnitus with suspected stroke or sudden neurological signs needs immediate referral.[3]
claims.answer:
There is a real kernel here. In some people, tinnitus gets louder, quieter or changes pitch when they clench the jaw, turn the head or press on certain muscles. Clinicians call this somatosensory (or somatic) tinnitus, because signals from the neck, jaw and face are interacting with the hearing system.

  • In a study of 121 tinnitus patients, 65% could change their tinnitus with muscle contractions of the head, neck or limbs; only 14% of 100 healthy volunteers could start a sound that way.[4]
  • But changing in the moment is not the same as stopping. In a clinic study of 81 patients, neck movements made tinnitus quieter in 30% and louder in 27%, and being able to modulate it did not predict a better outcome.[5]
  • Structured physiotherapy, jaw treatment or manual therapy, delivered over weeks by a trained clinician after assessment, helped some selected patients (people with tinnitus plus neck or jaw problems) in small trials. That is a treatment programme, not a 30-second trick.[6, 7, 8, 9]
subverdicts: “A 30-second neck or jaw move stops tinnitus”
Unsupported
No controlled study of a quick self-administered move was found. Maneuvers change tinnitus briefly in some people, and in some people make it worse.
“Tinnitus can change with neck or jaw movement”
Supported
Documented in several studies; more than half of the patients in some clinic and veteran samples showed it.
“Structured physiotherapy or jaw treatment can help some people”
Partly Supported

Several small randomised trials in selected patients with neck or jaw problems; low certainty, short follow-up. The German guideline recommends it for such patients; the 2026 U.S. guideline only suggests asking about somatosensory features.
“Neck cracking or chiropractic manipulation treats tinnitus”
Insufficient Evidence
Not adequately tested for tinnitus, and forceful neck manipulation has recognised rare risks.

sections: What somatosensory tinnitus is, and how common it may be

The brain’s hearing pathways receive input from the neck, jaw and facial nerves. In some people that input appears to feed into tinnitus. Experts only agreed international diagnostic criteria for it in 2018, after finding that differing definitions produced very different prevalence figures between studies.[10] One U.S. study of 304 veterans with tinnitus estimated that 56% (90% interval 45% to 65%) had a somatosensory component, using head, neck and jaw maneuvers as the screen.[11] Having the feature does not mean the maneuver is a treatment: it is a clue that a neck or jaw problem may be worth examining.
Why a quick move does not equal a treatment

In the clinic study of 81 patients, 62% showed some change with a neck or jaw maneuver. Neck maneuvers reduced loudness in about 30% and made it worse in about 27%; jaw maneuvers suppressed tinnitus in about 24%. Being able to modulate tinnitus, or being treated for it, was not related to improvement afterwards.[5] A brief change while a muscle is tensed says little about what happens when the muscle is released a minute later, and the studies of quick maneuvers we found measured changes during the maneuver, not lasting relief.
What structured treatment trials found

Several randomised trials tested treatment programmes, not quick moves:

  • Neck physiotherapy. In 38 people with tinnitus and neck complaints, 12 sessions over six weeks lowered tinnitus questionnaire scores. 53% reported substantial improvement right after treatment, and 24% still did six weeks later. The authors said larger studies were needed.[6]
  • Jaw (orofacial) treatment. In 80 people with jaw-related tinnitus, treatment with physiotherapy and, where needed, a bite splint, produced a larger clinically relevant improvement on one questionnaire (Tinnitus Functional Index) than delayed treatment; another questionnaire showed no clinically relevant reduction.[7]
  • Manual therapy. In 61 people with jaw-related tinnitus, adding hands-on neck and jaw therapy to exercise and education gave better tinnitus-severity and handicap scores than exercise and education alone, assessed by a blinded examiner.[8]
  • Trigger-point treatment. In 71 people with muscle pain and tinnitus, ten sessions of real trigger-point deactivation gave more tinnitus relief than sham treatment in a double-blind trial.[9]

Reviews are cautious. A 2016 review of six studies called the risk of bias high.[12] A 2023 review of four trials in jaw-related tinnitus found that physiotherapy reduced tinnitus intensity or severity, with low certainty.[13]
What the guidelines say

The two guidelines say different things, and neither recommends a self-applied quick move.

  • The 2026 U.S. guideline says clinicians may ask about somatosensory features (for example, whether tinnitus changes with jaw or neck movement) in people with persistent, bothersome tinnitus. That is a statement about taking a history. The executive summary lists no recommendation for physiotherapy, manual therapy or neck manipulation.[14]
  • The German guideline goes further and recommends offering manual and physiotherapeutic treatment when examination shows that tinnitus is modulated by findings in the neck or jaw, while noting the low methodological rigour and heterogeneity of the trials behind it.[15]

So the studies above evaluate treatment programmes in selected patients, and the U.S. guideline’s “ask about it” option should not be read as endorsing physiotherapy or neck manipulation.
distinctions: Maneuvers can lower, raise or not change loudness briefly. In treatment trials, some people reported lower severity after weeks of therapy.
How much does it bother me?
Questionnaire scores improved in several small trials of structured treatment, often alongside neck or jaw pain improvement.
Does it affect sleep, work or daily life?
Measured by questionnaires such as the Tinnitus Functional Index; benefits were modest and not always clinically relevant.
Seen in some people during or just after a maneuver. Others get worse.
Some people after a treatment programme; follow-up was short (for example six weeks).
Not shown. No study reports tinnitus eliminated by a quick move.
claims.limits: Trials in this area are small (38 to 80 people), usually cannot blind participants, often use a delayed-start comparison rather than a sham, and use different treatments and questionnaires, so they are hard to combine. Reviews rate the risk of bias as high or the certainty as low. Follow-up is short. Diagnostic criteria for somatosensory tinnitus were only agreed in 2018, so older studies defined it differently. Studies of the “instant” maneuvers shown in videos are essentially absent.
claims.coi: Tinnitus Evidence is independently operated, takes no advertising or affiliate payments, and sells no treatment. Several of the videos described above were posted by clinics or practitioners who offer neck, spine or jaw services, which gives them a commercial interest in the claim. Some of the trials cited were run by research groups that also deliver the treatment studied; each study page on this site records funding where it is reported.
claims.practical:
• Notice whether jaw clenching, neck turning or pressing near the ear changes your tinnitus, and tell your clinician. Gentle observation is low-risk; forceful pulling, twisting or cracking is not.
  • Ask for a proper assessment first: a hearing test and an ear, jaw and neck examination.[14] If neck or jaw findings are present, a physiotherapist or dentist experienced in jaw and neck disorders can design a programme for you, and teach exercises that are safe for your neck.
  • If jaw clenching or teeth grinding is part of the picture, a dentist can assess it and discuss options such as a bite splint.[7]
  • Whatever the cause, approaches that reduce how much tinnitus bothers you, such as cognitive behavioural therapy and, with hearing difficulties, a hearing-aid assessment, remain the best-supported options.[14]
claims.notes: No controlled trial of a self-applied 30-second maneuver was found in the sources reviewed; the statement is “none found”, not “none exist”. Re-run a PubMed search before publication.

claims.question: Do Vitamins, Herbs, or “Ear Formula” Supplements Work for Tinnitus?
claims.claim: “A natural vitamin, herb or ear formula can repair your ears or brain and stop the ringing, and doctors recommend it.”
claims.verdictLine: No supplement has been shown, in repeated good-quality trials, to relieve tinnitus. Some were tested without benefit; many marketed formulas were never tested. Unsupported is not the same as disproven.
claims.metaTitle: Do Vitamins, Herbs or Ear Formula Supplements Work for Tinnitus? | Tinnitus Evidence
claims.metaDesc: Ginkgo, zinc, magnesium, B12, Lipo-Flavonoid and marketed ear formulas: what trials and 2026 guidelines say, which were tested without benefit and which were never tested.
claims.answer:
Supplements are among the most heavily advertised tinnitus products, and the evidence behind them is thin.

  • Guidelines: the 2026 U.S. guideline says clinicians “should not recommend dietary supplements” for persistent, bothersome tinnitus.[1] The 2019 European guideline recommends against them[2] and the German guideline says they “are to be omitted”.[3]
  • Tested, no benefit shown: ginkgo, zinc and vitamin B12 were each compared with placebo and did not show a reliable benefit.[4, 5, 6]
  • Inadequately tested: magnesium (one small, unpublished placebo-controlled result that showed no difference, plus an open-label study),[7] bioflavonoid formulas and most branded “ear formulas” have little or no adequate placebo-controlled evidence.
  • One exception worth knowing: a single manufacturer-funded trial of one multi-ingredient formula beat placebo on a handicap questionnaire; it has not been independently repeated.[8]

“Unsupported” here covers two different situations, and the table below keeps them apart: tested without benefit and not adequately tested.
subverdicts: “A supplement can cure or reverse tinnitus”
Unsupported
No trial shows it; the 2026 U.S. guideline advises against recommending supplements.
“Ginkgo helps tinnitus”
Unsupported
Tested in many trials; Cochrane found little to no effect, with very uncertain evidence.
“Zinc helps tinnitus”
Unsupported
Tested against placebo; no significant benefit.
“Vitamin B12 helps tinnitus”
Unsupported
A 140-person double-blind trial found no difference from placebo.
“Magnesium helps tinnitus”
Insufficient Evidence

The only placebo-controlled result we found is a small, unpublished registry posting that showed no difference and reports no between-group test; an earlier open-label study had no placebo group. Too limited to conclude either way.
“Marketed ear formulas work, and doctors recommend them”
Insufficient Evidence
One formula has one sponsor-run placebo-controlled trial; most were never tested. Advertising claims have been challenged.

sections: Ingredient by ingredient

This table separates what has been tested from what has not. It is a summary of the best evidence we checked, not an exhaustive list.

Evidence for individual supplements and formulas in tinnitus
Ingredient or product typeBest evidence foundWhere it stands
Ginkgo bilobaCochrane review (2022): 12 trials, 1,915 people. Pooled data from two studies suggested little to no effect on tinnitus severity; the evidence was very uncertain.[4]Tested little or no effect shown
ZincCochrane review (2016): 3 trials, 209 people, moderate to high risk of bias. The one trial using a validated questionnaire (elderly adults, 50 mg a day for 4 months) found that 5% improved meaningfully on zinc and 2% on placebo, not a significant difference.[5, 10]Tested no benefit shown
Vitamin B12Double-blind trial of 140 people with tinnitus: no significant difference from placebo on handicap or visual-analogue severity scores at 1 or 3 months.[6]Tested no benefit shown
MelatoninPlacebo-controlled crossover trial of 30 people: the difference in handicap scores between melatonin and placebo was not significant. The authors saw a possible benefit in people whose tinnitus disturbed sleep, a subgroup finding in one small trial.[11]Tested no overall benefit; sleep subgroup untested
MagnesiumA randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial at Mayo Clinic (38 enrolled) posted its results only to the trial registry: tinnitus distress ratings after magnesium (5.36 out of 10) and after placebo (5.46), and average handicap scores (24.1 and 23.2), were essentially the same.[7] An earlier open-label study of 26 people (19 completed) at the same centre, with no placebo group, had reported lower scores.[12]Small, unpublished no difference in the one placebo-controlled result found; too limited for a firm conclusion
Lipo-Flavonoid (bioflavonoid formula)The only randomised study we found used it as the comparison treatment (40 people, 12 dropped out); the authors could not conclude it works. We found no placebo-controlled trial. Advertising claims about it were reviewed by an industry self-regulatory board in 2016.[13, 14]Inadequately tested
One multi-ingredient formula with a placebo-controlled trial114 adults analysed; handicap score fell by 13.2 points on the formula versus 6.2 on placebo over 3 months (p = 0.016). The trial was manufacturer-funded, and we found no independent repeat. Because many ingredients were combined, it cannot show which, if any, helped.[8]Early, single, sponsor-run trial
Most branded “ear formulas” and dropsA survey of over-the-counter tinnitus products found that all made unfounded relief claims and most were mixtures of inexpensive, common vitamins, minerals and herbs sold at a premium.[15] We found no tinnitus study of most branded formulas.Untested
Reviews that pool the evidence

A 2026 systematic review of nine randomised trials (390 adults) of over-the-counter oral treatments, including melatonin, ginkgo, alpha-lipoic acid, açaí and combination formulas, concluded that findings were “inconsistent and limited”, placebo responses were common, most products were studied in only one small trial, and no firm conclusions could be drawn about whether any provides benefit.[16] A 2025 network meta-analysis of 60 drug and supplement trials ranked ginkgo with vitamins first for tinnitus severity, but the certainty of that evidence was very low and the analysis found several inconsistent comparisons, so the authors described such antioxidants only as “promising” and called for better trials.[17]

Observational surveys can mislead too. A U.S. national survey linked low blood manganese, but not low zinc or vitamin B12, with more frequent and more disruptive tinnitus. The authors read this as a reason for further research, not as proof that taking a supplement helps.[18]
What regulators do and do not check

In the United States, supplement makers may describe an effect on the body’s structure or function without FDA pre-approval; these claims must carry a notice that FDA has not evaluated them and that the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease.[19] A 2019 survey of over-the-counter tinnitus remedies noted that some brands advertise in ear, nose and throat journals and prominently feature supposed endorsement by ENT doctors; the authors described the remedies as unproven.[15]

A documented example: in 2016 the advertising industry’s National Advertising Review Board recommended that the maker of one bioflavonoid supplement stop claims that it eases or quiets the ringing. It found support only for the narrower statement that the product “may provide relief for some people who suffer from tinnitus”. A recommendation to modify advertising is not a finding of wrongdoing.[14]
Safety: “natural” does not mean risk-free

The 2019 European guideline says dietary and alternative therapies “pose potential harm” as well as lacking proven efficacy.[2] The German guideline notes that ginkgo can interact with blood thinners and increase bleeding risk in people with clotting problems.[3] The Cochrane review found little to no difference in bleeding or seizure risk in trials, with low certainty.[4] Ask a pharmacist or doctor before combining any supplement with other medicines.
distinctions: No supplement has been shown to reduce loudness reliably. Where loudness was measured (ginkgo, zinc), differences were not significant and certainty was very low.
How much does it bother me?
A few trials report lower questionnaire scores, but placebo groups often improve too.[16]
Little evidence either way. Some melatonin data hint at a sleep subgroup; this has not been tested properly.
Personal reports are common; they cannot be told apart from expectation or natural change.
Not shown for any supplement in independently repeated trials.
No supplement has been shown to cure tinnitus.
claims.limits: Most supplement trials are small and short, use different doses, formulas and questionnaires, and some report only before-and-after changes without a placebo group. Some have been run or funded by the product’s maker. For the individual ingredients above, “no benefit shown” means that the best available trials did not detect one, which is not proof that no individual could ever benefit. Several widely sold formulas have never been tested in people with tinnitus, so no conclusion can be drawn about them either way. Some details on funding come from the study report itself and from our Emerging page records; we flag where they have not been independently confirmed.
claims.coi: Tinnitus Evidence is independently operated, carries no advertising or affiliate links, sells no supplements and receives no payment from any maker named here. We name a product or company only where a regulator, a published study or a documented fact-check supports the specific statement. Several of the trials above were funded by the product’s manufacturer, which we say where the study reports it. The Cochrane reviews were not.
claims.practical:
• Before spending money, ask what the label claims, whether a trial of that exact product in people with tinnitus exists, and who paid for it. “Doctor recommended” and “clinically proven” need a named study.
  • Do not stop prescribed medicines for a supplement. Tell your doctor or pharmacist what you take, especially ginkgo with blood thinners.[3]
  • If a blood test shows a deficiency of a vitamin or mineral, treating it is a separate medical decision, not a tinnitus treatment.
  • If tinnitus bothers you, the better-supported options reduce distress: cognitive behavioural therapy and, with hearing difficulties, hearing aids.[1]
  • If someone endorses a product with a celebrity or a “Harvard discovery”, check the claim on a fact-checking site before paying.[9]

claims.question: Have Scientists Discovered a Tinnitus Cure or Its “Real Cause”?
claims.claim: “Researchers have just discovered a cure for tinnitus, or the one real cause of it, and a treatment is almost here.”
claims.verdictLine: Real research is under way and some of it is promising, but no cure has been shown in people, and tinnitus does not have a single “real cause”. Unsupported does not mean the research is worthless.
claims.metaTitle: Has a Tinnitus Cure or “Real Cause” Been Discovered? How to Read Headlines | Tinnitus Evidence
claims.metaDesc: How tinnitus breakthrough headlines grow from animal studies and pilots, what research really shows, a worked example of a viral post, and a short checklist for readers.
claims.answer:
New tinnitus discoveries are published every week, and many are genuine. Headlines turn them into “cure” or “real cause” stories by skipping the steps in between.

  • No cure has been shown. No treatment has been shown to remove tinnitus in controlled, repeated trials. Regulators have authorised devices for temporary relief or “relief of tinnitus”, not cure.[1, 2] A 2021 review put it plainly: “neither full understanding, nor cure exists”.[3]
  • There is no single “real cause”. Tinnitus is most often set off by hearing loss and kept going by changes in brain networks; exactly what is necessary and sufficient is still being worked out.[3]
  • Most discoveries are early. They are mouse results, differences measured in blood, or small pilot studies. The table below shows where they sit.

This is not a reason to ignore research. It is a reason to ask what step a finding has reached before believing a headline.
subverdicts: “A cure for tinnitus has been discovered”
Unsupported
No controlled, replicated study shows a cure. Early findings exist; none demonstrates one.
“Scientists have found the real cause of tinnitus”
Misleading
Several mechanisms are being studied; hearing loss plus brain-network changes is the usual picture. No single cause explains all tinnitus.
“Nerve stimulation cured tinnitus in clinical trials” (worked example)
Unsupported
The best controlled data are a small pilot that did not show a significant group difference.
“Early research may point to future treatments”
Partly Supported
True for several animal and early human findings, as leads rather than treatments.

sections: What a “cure” would have to show

For a claim that something cures tinnitus to hold up, people would need to be shown to lose their tinnitus and stay free of it, compared with a control group, and the result would need repeating by independent teams, with a regulator or guideline panel then reviewing it. None of that exists for tinnitus. In its 2026 guideline the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Foundation recommends cognitive behavioural therapy and hearing-aid evaluation, advises against dietary supplements and magnetic stimulation, and treats sound enrichment and bimodal neuromodulation as options; it does not describe any cure.[5]
Why “the real cause” keeps being “found”

A 2021 review in Physiological Reviews describes tinnitus as, in most cases, initiated by acquired hearing loss and maintained when that loss is coupled with distinct neuronal changes in auditory and non-auditory brain networks, with the exact mechanisms still incompletely understood.[3] Each new finding about one part of this picture (a circuit, a protein, an inflammation signal) can be reported as “the cause” when it is one piece. A blood marker that differs between groups, for example, may reflect hearing loss or noise exposure rather than cause tinnitus; the 2026 prestin studies adjusted for age, hearing thresholds and noise exposure, and their authors describe a candidate biomarker, not a cause or a treatment.[6, 7]
How a finding climbs from lab to clinic

Use this ladder to place any headline. Most “breakthrough” stories describe step 1 or 2.

How far a tinnitus finding has travelled, from animal study to regulator decision
StepWhat it meansWhere tinnitus findings sit
1. Animal or cell studyShows a mechanism or a drug effect in mice, rats, gerbils or cells. Most such findings do not carry over to people.A serotonin circuit linked to tinnitus-like behaviour in mice (2026);[8] a drug that reduced tinnitus-like behaviour in gerbils (2025);[9] inflammation signals in noise-exposed mice (2019).[10]
2. Measured in people, no treatmentA difference between people with and without tinnitus. An association, not a cause, and not a treatment.Higher blood levels of an inner-ear protein, prestin, in two 2026 studies of 89 and 82 people;[6, 7] a screen of 96 inflammatory blood proteins in 548 people with tinnitus and 548 matched controls found no usable biomarker after correction for multiple testing.[11]
3. Small uncontrolled or pilot study in peopleEncouraging, but without a proper comparison group it cannot separate the treatment from time and expectation.Ten people with an implanted vagus-nerve stimulator: four had clinically meaningful improvement (2014).[12]
4. Controlled trialCompares treatment with placebo or another comparison. Tinnitus trials often show large placebo responses.An injected drug did not beat placebo in a phase 2 trial, with an “unexpectedly high placebo response” (2023);[13] a 30-person nerve-stimulation pilot found no significant difference between groups (2017).[14]
5. Independent repeatA different team, ideally larger, gets the same result. This is what makes a finding reliable.None for any proposed tinnitus cure.
6. Regulator decision or guidelineAn agency authorises a device or drug for a stated use, or a guideline recommends it.FDA-authorised devices are for temporary relief or “relief of tinnitus”, not cure.[1, 2]
A worked example: the “Northwestern cure” post

About 15 October 2026 we saw a Facebook post, from a page that shares science news, saying that Northwestern researchers had developed a vagus-nerve-stimulation therapy that cured chronic tinnitus. It was about 14 hours old when we saw it; we do not know how widely it spread. We are not naming or linking the page, because the claim matters, not the account.

Claims in a Facebook post about Northwestern University and tinnitus, compared with what we found
What the post saysWhat we found
“American doctors cured chronic tinnitus” in clinical trialsNo trial reports a cure. The best controlled human data on this approach are a 30-person pilot in which the difference between groups was not statistically significant, and small case series.[14, 12]
“Northwestern researchers developed” it; “Source: Northwestern University, 2025”We found no matching Northwestern study. Of 17 tinnitus papers from Northwestern authors in 2020-2026, none concerned vagus-nerve stimulation or sound pairing, and the university’s two registered tinnitus studies tested electrical stimulation through the scalp.[15, 16] The post names no paper, researcher or link. This is a “not found” result, not proof that no unpublished work exists.
“pairing sound with gentle electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve”This matches research from the University of Texas at Dallas, which began in rats in 2011 (tones paired with brief vagus-nerve pulses; effects in noise-exposed rats, not people).[17] Human studies followed: an implanted-stimulator case series (2014)[12] and a 30-person implanted pilot with industry-linked authors (2017).[14]
“a majority of participants reported significant improvement”In the 2017 pilot, 50% of the paired group and 28% of controls improved by a clinically meaningful amount after six weeks; the difference between groups was 10.3% and not statistically significant (p = 0.34). The authors called for a larger pivotal study.[14]
“no drug, no surgery, and no implant”The published human studies of this approach used implanted stimulators.[12, 14] Early non-invasive versions have not shown a group benefit: a 29-person controlled study of an ear-clip device found no improvement in loudness or frequency,[18] and a 30-person trial found no significant between-group differences in loudness or the Tinnitus Functional Index.[19]
“Researchers are now working to make the therapy widely available”The MicroTransponder paired-stimulation pilot registered for tinnitus finished in 2016, and a later University of Texas at Dallas follow-up study was withdrawn with no participants.[20, 21] The FDA approval of the same paired-stimulation platform is for stroke arm rehabilitation, not tinnitus.[22] Registered trials of non-invasive versions are recruiting or planned at other centres.[16]

What Northwestern authors have published on tinnitus is real but different: a 20-person pilot of scalp electrical stimulation with MRI (2024), designed to study brain mechanisms rather than to test a treatment,[23] and a 2026 preprint (not yet peer reviewed) on brain-imaging markers whose opening sentence says chronic tinnitus has “few effective treatments and no cure”.[24]

We cannot tell who wrote the post, why, or what source they used. The accurate summary is: the therapy described resembles University of Texas at Dallas research; we found no Northwestern version; and “cured” goes well beyond what any trial reports. We have not contacted Northwestern University or the page.

A short checklist for any breakthrough claim

1. Is a paper, researcher or registry number named? A famous university with no paper, name or link is a warning sign. Search PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov for the topic plus the institution.
  2. In whom was it tested? Mice, rats or cells are early steps. Look for human participants and how many.
  3. Compared with what? Tinnitus improves with placebo and with time, so a result without a control group proves little.
  4. Cured, or a questionnaire score? “Silence” needs numbers. Reduced distress is not the same as a quieter or absent sound.
  5. Who paid for it, and who sells it? Sponsor-run results need independent repeats.
  6. Has anyone else repeated it? One study is a lead, not an answer.
  7. Is it actually available? “Soon” needs a registered trial or a regulator decision you can look up.
  8. Is it built to be shared? Countdown claims, celebrity endorsements, “doctors don’t want you to know”, and an emotional last line are features of marketing. Check a fact-checking site before paying anything.[4]

claims.practical:

  • To follow real developments, see our pages on clinical trials and emerging treatments, which are checked against ClinicalTrials.gov every week.
  • If you are interested in a trial, read its registry record, and talk to your clinician. Only the research team can tell you whether you are eligible.
  • Be wary of any product or clinic sold on the strength of one study, a celebrity or a “discovery”. Treatments with the best current support are those that reduce distress.[5]

claims.question: Does Tinnitus Ever Go Away, or Is It Permanent?
claims.short: Does tinnitus go away, or is it permanent?
claims.claim: “Tinnitus is permanent and nothing helps,” or the opposite: “it will go away on its own if you wait.”
claims.verdictLine: Both blanket claims mislead. Most tinnitus that lasts for months tends to persist, some does fade or disappear, and how much it bothers you can often be reduced.
claims.metaTitle: Does Tinnitus Go Away, or Is It Permanent? What the Research Shows | Tinnitus Evidence
claims.metaDesc: Does tinnitus go away on its own? Long-term studies show most persists, about 1 in 5 resolves, and distress can often be reduced. Plus when sudden hearing loss needs urgent care.
claims.safety:
Important safety note: sudden hearing loss needs urgent medical evaluation, especially with new tinnitus. If your hearing drops or seems muffled over a few hours to about three days, in one ear or both, or new ringing starts together with a sudden change in hearing, do not wait to see whether it settles. The U.S. National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders says to treat sudden deafness symptoms as a medical emergency and to visit a doctor immediately; although about half of people recover some or all hearing spontaneously, delay can reduce the effectiveness of treatment when treatment is warranted.[1] UK NICE guidance says that a person with tinnitus whose hearing loss developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) in the past 30 days should be seen within 24 hours.[2] The 2019 AAO-HNSF sudden hearing loss guideline likewise stresses prompt recognition and management and discusses time-limited treatments, such as corticosteroids within 2 weeks of onset.[3]

Call emergency services right away (911 in the U.S.) if tinnitus comes with facial weakness, sudden severe vertigo or other signs of stroke, such as sudden numbness or weakness on one side, sudden confusion or trouble speaking, sudden trouble seeing, or a sudden severe headache.[2, 4] If tinnitus has you thinking about harming yourself, seek urgent help now: in the US call or text 988; elsewhere use your local emergency or crisis line (see crisis support). Clinical guidelines tell clinicians to ask about self-harm in people with bothersome tinnitus.[5]
claims.answer:
“It’s permanent” and “it will go away” each contain some truth, and each misleads when stated as a rule.

  • Very brief ringing is treated differently. The 2026 U.S. guideline excludes “transient ear noise”, a sudden ringing in one ear lasting under 5 minutes, because it does not typically need clinical management.[5]
  • Established tinnitus tends to persist. In a five-year study of older adults, tinnitus persisted in 82% of those who had it at the start.[6] In a UK study of adults followed for four years, 18% of those who reported tinnitus reported none at follow-up; of those who still had it, 9% were less bothered, 9% were more bothered and the rest were unchanged.[7]
  • How much it bothers you is different from whether it is there. Cognitive behavioural therapy and, for people with hearing difficulties, hearing aids are recommended in the 2026 U.S. guideline because they can reduce distress and daily impact even when the sound remains.[5]

No treatment has been shown to cure tinnitus, so “nothing can be done” is also wrong: a lot can be done about its impact.
subverdicts: “Tinnitus always goes away on its own”
Unsupported
In long-term studies most tinnitus that is present persists; resolution is “relatively uncommon”.
“Tinnitus is permanent and nothing can be done”
Misleading
It does persist for most people, but distress and daily impact can often be reduced.
“Some people’s tinnitus does go away”
Supported
About 1 in 5 people reporting tinnitus reported none four years later in a large UK cohort.
“Therapies can reduce how much tinnitus bothers you”
Partly Supported
Recommended in guidelines; effects are modest on average, vary by person, and long-term follow-up is thin.

sections: What long-term studies show

Two population studies followed people over several years.

  • Blue Mountains Hearing Study (Australia, older adults): over five years, tinnitus present at the start was still present in 81.6%. Among those with tinnitus that was only mildly annoying at the start, 39.6% became moderately annoying and 5.9% severely annoying by the follow-up. Hearing loss roughly doubled the odds of new tinnitus (odds ratio 2.13).[6]
  • UK Biobank (adults aged 40-69, about 4,700 retested after four years): 18.3% of those who had reported tinnitus reported none at retest; of those who still had it, 9% reported improvement and 9% said it had become more bothersome. The authors concluded that resolution is relatively uncommon, and that improvement and worsening are equally likely.[7]

These are surveys of self-reported tinnitus, so some “resolution” may be fluctuation, and neither study followed people treated with a particular therapy. For most people, established tinnitus does not simply disappear; for some, it fades or becomes much less noticeable.
Why “permanent” is also an overstatement

Two things get blurred: whether the sound is present, and whether it is a problem. A national guideline asks clinicians to distinguish people who are bothered by tinnitus from people who are not, and educate patients about its natural history and ways to manage it.[5] Many people live with tinnitus that does not trouble them. For those it does trouble, several approaches have evidence:

  • Cognitive behavioural therapy. A Cochrane review of 12 studies (966 people) found CBT may reduce the impact of tinnitus on quality of life compared with other active treatments (small average effect, low certainty), and no evidence yet on effects at 6 or 12 months.[8] The 2019 European guideline gives it a strong recommendation.[9]
  • Hearing aids. For people with hearing loss, the 2026 U.S. guideline recommends a hearing-aid evaluation[5] and NICE says to offer amplification devices if hearing loss affects communication.[2] A Cochrane review found the evidence on hearing aids for tinnitus limited.[10]
  • Combination treatment. In a 461-person multicentre trial, every arm improved by week 12 on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory; CBT and hearing aids alone had large effects that combining treatments did not clearly add to.[11]

Improvement in these studies is mainly in distress and daily impact, not in the sound disappearing.
What this means for “cure” and “wait and see” claims

“It will go away on its own” can delay getting hearing checked or treated, and can hide a treatable cause such as sudden hearing loss. “It’s permanent and nothing helps” can discourage people from the approaches most likely to make life easier. A balanced message is that tinnitus often persists, sometimes fades, and its impact can usually be reduced.
distinctions: Some people report it fading over time; most with persisting tinnitus do not. Treatments rarely change loudness reliably.
How much does it upset or worry me?
The main target of CBT and related therapies, which can reduce it even if the sound stays.
Improves with therapy and, where there is hearing loss, with hearing aids in many people.
Common with sound, relaxation and time; fluctuates.
Seen in a proportion of people over time (9% of those who still had tinnitus reported improvement in the UK cohort) and after therapy; follow-up in trials is often short.
About 18% of people reporting tinnitus reported none at four years in one cohort (natural resolution, not a treatment effect); no treatment has been shown to cure it.
claims.limits: The long-term data come from two population cohorts that relied on self-report and used single questions about tinnitus; their populations (older Australians; UK adults aged 40-69) may not match yours, and attrition between visits could bias the figures. Neither tested treatments. Trials of CBT and hearing aids are heterogeneous and usually follow people for weeks to months. Our percentage figures are as reported by the studies, not our own estimates, and different studies define “tinnitus” and “bothersome” differently.

claims.practical:
• If tinnitus is new, one-sided, pulsing, or comes with hearing change or dizziness, get it checked. Start with a hearing test.[5]
  • If it has lasted beyond a few weeks and bothers you, ask your doctor or audiologist about support: tinnitus education, cognitive behavioural therapy (including online programmes), and a hearing-aid assessment if your hearing has changed.[2]
  • Do not judge a treatment by whether the sound disappears. Ask whether sleep, concentration, mood and daily life improve.
  • Be wary of anyone promising to switch tinnitus off, or telling you it is hopeless. Both ignore what the evidence shows.
